title: Vowels, diphthongs and iota subscript

objectives.can: Tell long vowels from short, recognise the diphthongs, and read a vowel with iota subscript.

explanation.summary: Greek has seven vowel letters. Some are always short, some always long, and some may be either. Two vowels can join into one syllable (a diphthong), and a long vowel may carry a small iota underneath. Knowing these lets you see where one syllable ends and the next begins.

sections.heading: Seven vowels, long and short
body: Greek vowels are short or long. Ε and ο are always short. Η and ω are always long, and they are the long partners of ε and ο: epsilon is the short e and eta the long e; omicron is the short o and omega the long o. The three vowels α, ι and υ may be short or long, and the letter does not tell you which.

The length of α, ι and υ is not marked in ordinary printed texts. You learn it with the word, and it is only needed for a few matters, such as where accents may stand (lesson G0.2.2). The vowel table in this lesson gives the letters with their length and school sound.

sections.heading: Diphthongs
body: A diphthong is a pair of vowels read as one syllable. The common ones are αι, ει, οι, υι, αυ, ευ, ου and, more rarely, ηυ. The second vowel is ι or υ in every case. In καί the letters α and ι make one syllable; in εἰς, ε and ι make one; in οὐρανός the letters ο and υ make the single syllable ου.
Two vowels side by side do not always form a diphthong. Only the pairs listed make one. The letters ω and η in ζωή, for example, are two vowels in two syllables.
Each diphthong has a sound in the school convention, shown in the diphthong table. Lesson G0.3.1 shows that other traditions pronounce several of them differently.

sections.heading: Iota subscript
body: Three long vowels may have a small ι written beneath them: ᾳ, ῃ and ῳ. This is the iota subscript. You see it in σκοτίᾳ, in ἀρχῇ and in κόσμῳ. It is part of the spelling and it changes the form of the word, but in the school convention it is not pronounced.

The iota was once written in line after the vowel, and by the time of the New Testament it was no longer pronounced in most speech. The subscript is the later way of showing it. In some printed texts a capital vowel carries its iota beside it on the line instead of beneath.

sections.heading: Diaeresis: two dots
body: Two dots over ι or υ show that this vowel is read separately from the one before it and does not join it. In Μωϋσέως the dots on the υ show that the ω and the υ are separate syllables. In πρωΐ the dots on the ι stop it from being read as an iota subscript or as a diphthong with ω.

misunderstandings: A diphthong is one syllable, not two. The two letters of ει are one sound, not 'e' followed by 'i'.
Two vowels together are not necessarily a diphthong. Check the list: αι, ει, οι, υι, αυ, ευ, ου, ηυ. Two other vowels in a row, such as ω and η, are separate syllables.
The iota subscript is not an accent and not a breathing. It is a small ι that belongs to the vowel above it.
α, ι and υ are not 'short vowels'. The letter alone does not say whether they are long or short.

deeper.heading: Long and short in the history of Greek
body: In the classical language, vowel length was a real distinction: a long vowel took about twice as long to say as a short one. Over the following centuries the difference of length faded from the spoken language, though the spelling kept the letters. This lesson teaches the written distinction, which is what you need to read the texts.

examples.analysis: θεόν has two short vowels, ε and ο. λόγος has two short omicrons. ἀρχῇ ends in η, a long vowel, and it carries an iota subscript, so its last letter is ῃ. Count the vowels in each word as you read: each vowel here is a syllable of its own.

examples.analysis: τῇ and σκοτίᾳ both carry the iota subscript: the first is η with a subscript, the second α with a subscript. Together they read 'in the darkness'. Both words are in the dative case, which you meet later and where the subscript is common; you need not pronounce it.

examples.analysis: Μωϋσέως has two dots over the υ. They show that the υ is read apart from the preceding ω, in a separate syllable. πρωΐ is written here as πρωῒ with a grave accent on the ι; the dots on the ι keep it separate from the ω, so that the pair is not read as the single letter ῳ. Two dots over a vowel are the diaeresis.
